segments.words: Well, so the landing is so filled up that you can't send a bull hook back to the woods and get more logs. You're just filled up, you know. Was he trying to...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He was trying to block you?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yes, I think he was. Well, we had two days left for that setting. And next to the last day, there wasn't hardly any logs came down. We didn't do a darn thing that day. Not a thing. Once, I think there was one or two drags came down. And I didn't know what the hell was the matter. And then the last day, that was going to be his last day, the bull hook could go up into the woods and... Here a drag had come down and we'd unfastened him and the bull hook could go back up into the woods. And here's another drag. What he did, he yarded out all these logs the day before so he could block me. He never did learn my name. He did. And I just threw my peavey, you understand? And he must have been watching me from trees way up in the hill. Because when he seen me start down the railroad track for camp, he came running and waving his arms. Hey boy, hey boy, wait a minute boy, hey boy. I said, fuck you, you goddamn Pollack son of a bitch. And no, I never took shit from nobody those days. And you know, he never could learn my name. I just had to take my time and I let Tony... You know, the name was Tony Burch. He was a Pollack. He had to clean up his own landing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was his job?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: He was the boss for the whole thing. He was hooked and he was the big shop. He was boss for the whole thing and I was boss on the landing. He under him. Yeah. Only as a rule, the hook tender didn't have too much to say about what was going on on the landing. The hook, the top loader was boss on the landing. He never did learn. Lots of times years after he'd seen me on the... He finally got married. And he lived in Bole. And lots of times he'd seen me on the train going by, you know. Oh, hello there boy, hello boy. He never did learn my name.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why not… i wondered why I couldn't. I guess he just didn't like you, huh?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, he liked me. Oh, he did. Oh, yes, he liked me. I've seen him afterwards. He acted like he lost, like I was one of his long lost friends.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, gee, there weren't many poles in the woods, were there? Around the Upper River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No… not very many Pollacks. No. No. No, not very many Pollacks. Not a lot of Yugoslavians. ... And... He'd always say, hello Swede. I said, hello, seven inch. I always wondered, I wondered if he's using that as a slur word. Because I'm not ashamed of being a Swede. He was kind of sticking in my craw. One day when I met him on the street, he said, hello Swede. Oh, hello, Bo Hunk. My God, you know, it was always hello George after that… you know… that's why I never got into a fight, but generally took care of it before the start.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Before it reached that point.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.words: I guess it was Ma Vine that was telling me some about the... That the Austrians in town had big bootlegs.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, there was one Austrian there. Povich was one, she said. Oh yeah, Joe Povich. He was the big bootlegger in town. Oh yeah… yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wonder where he got it from.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: They brought it in by car at night.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You think all the way from Spokane or some place like that or...

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah oh yeah. They brought it in there. And some of it was moonshine. There's some moonshiners down on the river Baden. What was their name now?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I heard there was some of the ...

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, I think there was some of the ... too, but there was that... That's what that fella's name. Well, it's a blank now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They get it from him too. They get it from this guy too?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh yeah. Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Then would they sell it to all the lumberjacks no matter whether they were Swedes or whatever their nationality was? Oh yeah. They were just big suppliers. The moonshiners. The Austrians and Povich and those.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, no, Povich, he bootlegged. Oh yes, he bootlegged. Can't think of that guy's name down on the river. He moonshined. And he's also the guy that killed. segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he say why he'd done it?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: He thought he was squealing on him for moonshining.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did this guy from Dent supply a lot of the lumberjacks around Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. Oh yeah. Yeah, he used to bring, um, more, I guess, uh, 15, 20 gorges. Over.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It'll come to you when you're not thinking of it, you know.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: That's right. That's right. That's right. Well, if you ever find out who those, there were two brothers, I think, of them. And they were, they were suppliers. And, uh... Oh my god, I can't think. I heard that some of that, some moonshine was really bad stuff. Most of it was good, but some of it was terrible. Oh yeah. Oh, some of it was terrible. Oh yeah… jenks. Ira Jenks.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: J-E-N-K-S or...

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: And, uh..… and he didn't want no drink, and when they got down to around the point, Frank could hear Tom Howard say to him, Jenks says, Didn't you know he don't drink? Well, I didn't know he looks human. He should drink.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wonder if these Jenks boys came from the south, because, you know, quite a bit of that good moonshine I understood was made by folks that come from there.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: They came from Virginia. That whole outfit, and all those Snyder's and Carr's and Bonner's and stuff up above our phenom, they're all from the... Virginians. They're all Virginians. West Virginians.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, I was going to ask you about the clan, the Ku Klux Klan in Elk River.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I'll tell you, I think they were pretty strong during the First World War. segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, I heard that they'd burned some crosses around Elk River.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I heard that they did, but it didn't happen while I was there. It happened while I was out in the shipyards. segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah. That had just about died out, I think. I hope so. It sounded like I could never figure out from what I heard what they were trying to do. I mean, in the South, I know they were against the Blacks, and they wanted to try to keep them down, you know.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, I tell you, during Reconstruction, you know, after the Civil War, I guess the carpetbaggers from up north really raised hell with the white people down south. And they had to just do something. And they just about had to start something, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But then, out here, it was, I mean, there were no Black people to speak of, so it must have been, see, I'd heard it was against Catholics, and I guess maybe that was the main thing they had going out here, was against the Catholic people. You know, we were talking about Malcher Anderson before, and about his wife, and you were saying she didn't have enough sense to come in out of the rain, his wife. I was wondering, I still can't figure out, and other people have talked to me about her, I still don't understand what was so strange about her, what made her such a crazy kind of person. Was she a loose woman?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, no, no, no. She just didn't have any sense, she just didn't have good sense, you know. I'd say... Well, I'd say that she was slightly retarded, let's put it that way.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was she kind of childish?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah… well, I just wanted, for instance, if she had to go someplace, when she had a baby this time. And I forget now, what she used to... if it was turpentine or something that she'd put on this baby's vagina, she'd have smart, so she'd urinate before she left, so she wouldn't urinate in bed. Now, what do you think of that?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's terrible, for the kid.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I understand that... that girl... now I heard of that, I heard here about a year ago that she's... she's grown up now, and I think she's been married, but she thinks she's complete alcoholic. She's absolutely gone.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was she a good looking woman?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, in talking... I hear a lot about the Hobos, guys that were, you know, bumming around in the 20s and in the Depression. Oh, yeah. And I've heard too that the lumberjacks that were out of work, couldn't get jobs, could wind up having to do the same thing, themselves.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah. Oh, I'll tell you, after I... I just quit paying the railroad fare for quite a while. You know, if I wanted to go someplace, I'd catch a freight. Yeah. Like when I worked out on the coast, like I told you, when Minnie came to camp with her girls. When I got word that they wanted me to work in a cleaning mill in Kamiah up here, I took the freight to Saint Maries. I didn't. I didn't pay no railroad fare. But when I got to Saint Maries, I think I bought my ticket from Saint Maries to... No, wait a minute now… i bought..… i bought my way to Saint Maries on the freight and seen him. And then we went to Spokane on the Milwaukee and then we took Dan and Pete to Kamiah. But I never paid anything between... between Hoquiam  and Saint Maries. I just rode the freight.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It was easy to get... it was easy to get on and stay on?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. It wasn't always easy going east. Generally going east they're loaded. But going west they're empty. You can just be afraid going west any time. But going east they're pretty loaded. Generally pretty loaded.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There are usually a lot of guys going riding when you were on.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Lots of time. You know, one time I worked in Saint Maries. And there was an old Swede by the name of Gus Benson, was Greenlumber Foreman. And at that time Idaho was dry. I don't know now. No. It was... I think it was local option. Benoit County was dry. That's the way it was. But you could get wished in Saltice, Montana, just over the line, you know. And nobody, all those Swede lumber pilots and stuff, they didn't know a darn thing about beating a freight. I was the only one. I had an Iso-Saltice, and a five gallon whiskey. And Gus Benson, the foreman, he had to have some of it in the rest of them. But he paid my wages all the time while I was gone. And you know, what it was like this. Here's the Lumber, here's Harry's Lumber Yard. Like so. Here's the Saint Maries River. And the railroad comes like this, around the Lumber Yard and into town. And the boarding house was over here. And the freight, as it comes along in the morning, always pulls toward the Indian, just about into the railroad yard. And the freight is strung up all along the Lumber Yard. So all I had to do was just jump out of the box car and walk through the Lumber Yard and into the boarding house, where we were staying. You know, I walked through the Lumber Yard. Nobody to stop you, nothing, you know. And there was nothing to it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What town was this by?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Saint Maries… yeah, there. Yeah… the Lumber Yard, the Saint Maries River runs like so. And, let's see now, yeah. And here's the town of Saint Maries. Here's the town of Saint Maries. Here's Herrick's Lumber Yard. And the railroad track comes like this. And into the freight yards. Well, the boarding house where we stayed was here. But always every morning that freight would stop like so. Dead stop. And all I had to do was just jump out of the box car and walk through the Lumber Yard and into the boarding house. And we were to it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you be able to get up to Salties and back the next day? When you'd go?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. I took the passenger over to Salties.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, you didn't ride the freight?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, but I rode the freight coming back. I see. With a whiskey. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How often would you go?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, whenever Gus wanted to. I think I made about three trips that summer while we were there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And the rest of it was for the other guys?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how was the drinking done by the men then? Would they do it just at nights when work day was over?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, is that when they drink?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah… over weekends, generally. I was running into it mostly over weekends.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Not too much on a weeknight?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, no, no. No. There was a couple of card sharks in Elk River one time and this same Gus Pencil, he was green-lumber-forming up at Elk River at that time. The same guy that was down for Herrick when I used to bring the whiskey from Salties. Well, we were born with a Swede family there. And here was this John. I forget his last name. He was a lumber pilot or a husky guy. And every payday, these card sharks would get ahold of him and get his paychecks. He'd always hold off if he was bored and stuff, but they'd get the rest of it. And he was a hard worker. And finally Gus Pencil, his boss, he was bored in there too. He got after John. Told him what a darn fool he was to give his money away. And John, he listened to Gus. I guess there was three, four paydays. The card sharks didn't get him. And finally one Saturday, they got him and took it all away from him. And Gus heard about it. So John, he had a room. Him and his partner had a room with his family, but Gus had a room someplace else, but he always came down for his meals. And I had a shack of my own, and I came down. The breakfast table, I think it was on a Sunday morning, Gus had found out that John had lost all his money. So he started to give him the give him. And he really talked her to him. And John, he was insane.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yes, but God damn it, Gus, it was an awful God damn good game. What can you do with a guy like that?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Those guys really knew how to play good crooked poker, didn't they?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah. I never played. I never played. I know what I'm good at, and I don't know what I know how to do, and I don't know how to play poker. So I never played. I told you about Putman and the only Christian 20 minutes. You know, I was working with a fellow, and Gus was one of the hardest works and the biggest liars that I've ever known. His name was Putman. And Ed Lillard was the boss on the loading dock. He's retired, lived downtown here now. Well, Ed and I used to go fishing together a lot. All you had to do was just bring your pole and your basket down at noon and go up the creek a little ways after the whistle blew and get your 50 limit and go on home. There was no such a thing as, you just say, we're going to have fish for supper, and that was it. Well, you know, and Putman, he went fishing a lot too.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: And so he brought his pole down and his basket too. And he went fishing up the creek, but we never saw hide or hair after Ed and I went up. Well, how Ed and I fished the stream, and I fished his hole, Ed and he'd go by me to the next hole and fish, and I'd go and fish the next hole. That's the way we always do. You know, you don't hog it, you know. So Ed passed by me, and he stopped, and he said, God damn it, George, in the morning, let us ask Putman first. Well, he took it a little while to soak in, you know. But then I got to thinking, always when we went fishing, Putman had rushed up to Ed and I and asked us how many fish we'd caught, and we'd tell him, and he always caught more fish than we did. So, yeah, I said, by God we will. Well, Ed, he was the foreman, and it was in the morning, and Putman and I had already started to load lumber into this car. We were working contract. We got paid on, according to how much lumber we put in the car. Well, Ed was still putting up a few, you know, they have clipboards that go on every box car, shows what goes in each box car.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: And as he come by, he asked him, asked him, so I quit putting the lumber to Putman, and I went up and he said, how many fish did you catch yesterday, Putman? Well, I forget the count now, but I think he said 27 or something like that. And then, of course, he had to say, how many did you catch? Well, I said, I got 35 and Ed got 42. Yeah, but I only fished 20 minutes. And Ed just took one look at me, and he started to walk down that dock. He never said a goddamn word. Here, here, we had it all figured out, and we got beat anyway. My God, I tell you, that was one of the best words I've ever heard. And that's all Mr. God threw, there was a bit of it. You all see the look on Ed's face, I tell you. He just looked like it's no use. That's the expression he had on his face.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was Putman the kind of, was he as good a liar as Harry Adams?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No. No, he told such ridiculous lies. Harry Adams just told lies for fun.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But Putman told lies to build himself up.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. All this kind of, you know, brag at the years. He always had to walk the tip the best time or something like that, you know. He's always a little bit better than... Yeah. But you know, one time Ed and I had seen an ad in Sears Roebuck catalog. for these ... shoes. So I sent for a pair and Ed sent for a pair. And they were no good shoes, I tell you. And the islets frayed, you know. They'd eat up their shoestrings. And I was forever getting shoestrings for those shoes. This day, shoestring broke, and I can't stand the broken shoestring. And I went into Tyveen where we tied the number and got some of that twine. And made me enough so I'd get home, you know. And I was cussing those and got them shoestrings. And there was an old fellow there. He was a real gentleman, old man, Rowan. He'd been around, and he'd been a stool teacher, and he'd been a banker, and storekeeper, and homesteader. You know, I think he'd been telegraph operator and deep wagens on the railroad. And he was one of the best red men I've ever known.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Best what?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Red. He's red. Red, everything. And Rowan was there, and I was puttin' and I was headlittler than I, and I think there was a couple other guys standing around. And I was cussing those goddamn shoes that wore out so goddamn, and I can't keep shoestrings, these goddamn shoes. And I forget now. Well, Foote was like, you know, one time I had a pair of shoestrings, and you know, I wore out four pair of shoes with that one pair of shoestrings. And we all looked at each other. Nobody said a word. Nobody wanted to say, oh, you're a goddamn liar. We just kind of looked at each other kind of funny, and we ran away. Every time anything afterwards came up, that was kind of ridiculous. We'd say, well, that's just about as bad as Putman when he wore out four pair of shoes with that one pair of shoestrings. And each time he kept on looking down his nose a little more every time he was sprung, you know. And finally, one time, I was sprung and he said, my God, I never did say that.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: By that time, he'd seen how goddamn ridiculous it was, and he took it all back. Be fair, what you hear in a lifetime, maybe.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he a nice guy, Putman?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, he was a nice fellow. He was a nice fellow. Yeah. But he was, he was tighter than a bark on a tree. He was a nice fellow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Tighter, you mean with his money or with his...

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. Oh, yeah. He was tight, I tell you. One night, I was out in the moonlight. It was in June. In fact, it was the 4th of June. I was going to get me a banjo. I was in his homestead cabin. And I had my grain headache, I tell you, that was almost killing me. And I had a hole in the shades. I laid up in the attic and I had a hole in the shades. It was moonlight. And I had one of these mummy sleeping bags. I thought, I'll take one more look out in the meadow. If there's nothing, if I don't see anything, I'll just sleep tomorrow and see if anything comes in. So I looked out out of the shades and here came the biggest thing walking into the meadow you ever saw. And I was praying to Christ that it would be a deer buck, but when I pulled the trigger, I knew better. It was a bull elk… and, by God,… anyway, I got him. And there I was all alone with that goddamn big bull elk. But Putman had a car.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: And I went into town. I walked back into town and got Putman. And he else came on it. Oh my God, Putman. This thing is big. We gotta get bird. It's a young Swede. And he was at a dance. But we finally got bird. And we got washtubs and everything we could think of in the car and started down the street. The city marshal and the deputy sheriff stopped us and told us we forgot to turn our headlights on. But anyway, we went out. We went out and we had, we had damn near half a mile from where we left the car. We had almost half a mile to walk toward the elk laid in the meadow. And later I'd buy a fire patrol trail. And I'll tell you, we worked that night. Oh Jesus Christ, how we worked. But Putman could see why I wanted one more guy. When we came up to the, Jesus Christ, he's so that big. I'll tell you, that thing was big. Oh man. We packed meat, well we packed meat till daylight. When we delivered the meat to birds and my place in Putman's, it was daylight in the morning. The town wasn't up yet, but it was good daylight.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were, do you still have, do you have your migraine headache all through the night?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, it went away. After I got to, I ran into town and got to Sweatin' and that took it off, I think. Please, I had a headache, a groove on. I really had a headache. I got him up at Christianson Meadow, if you know where that is.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which Meadow?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Christianson Meadow… do you ever take the road up to Elk Butte?

segments.words: No, I've never been up there from Elk River, no.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Is it that Meadow that you pass, you go through a kind of a canyon and then you come out into an open Meadow. The road goes by, that Christus Meadow.

segments.words: You know, there's one thing I was going to ask you, I forgot about the whorehouses. The guys that got gonorrhea and that kind of thing, what did they treat it with?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, I'll tell you… you bet… yeah. I guess now all you have to do is take a couple of pills and it's over with. That's what I think, I don't think it's a big deal anymore. Oh, I understand. I don't know if it's or penicillin or, I guess syphilis is nothing to it anymore… isn't it… i don't know. I don't hear much about it these days. No, I think and penicillin cure both of them. I don't know which is which, but those guys that had gonorrhea, oh God. Oh. ... Oh yes, and I'll tell you, it took money to get cured. I was just lucky. I was just lucky. And it was rampant those days.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: A lot of guys got it... Well, how, for like most of the single men in the camps, how often would they wind up going to the whorehouses? Would they go fairly regular?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Some of them did, went fairly regular, and some of them just went once in a while. I guess some of them never went at all. They never got the urge. Know one guy. I was working loading cars in Saint Maries for Harry's. And you see, about this time of the year, nice sunshiny days, you know, there was a meadow on the other side of the boxcar. And I used to go out and lay in that meadow and eat my lunch. And with his young sweet, him and another fellow, they were batching in a little house about a quarter of a mile from the meadow. And he went home for dinner, and when he seen me laying in the grass there, he came over to me. And he said, you know, Jones, he said, I think I got a dose for class. Well, let's see, I said, so he, I'll lay this way, and he laid right off in it from me and opened up his pants and, oh, Jesus Christ, Mr. Man, I said, you better get this old can and get away. Well, he said, he told me afterwards by the time he got a room at the Galax Hotel, that isn't there, that's the parking lot now. His pants are wet, clear down from the discharge. And I guess he really had it. He really had it. I guess he was happy enough with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There was a place you could go for treatment in Spokane?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, there were doctors in Spokane. They would treat it. But, Jesus Christ, I guess the treatment was really something.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wonder how they treated it.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I don't know. I don't know. I heard one guy tell that they had something that they stuck in there. Then they pushed or something, and two or three little knives came out and ripped it open.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Sounds pretty bad… i kind of wondered why. I hear a lot about blowing in going to Spokane. I was wondering what would be the difference? Was there some guys that would just say, just go to Elk River or just hang around? Other guys that would go all the way to Spokane and blow in? Or did everybody go to Spokane once in a while to blow in?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, and then you went to work. You'd go to Spokane, and then you'd go off from there and work someplace else. You know, there was work every place those days. You'd say, well, I think that you didn't say, I'm going to go up to the standpoint and see if I can get a job. You'd just say, I'm going to go up to the standpoint and work a while. You're over-tucked alone… that's noble.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When guys blew in, though, I had the idea that they had to spend all their money. It wasn't like a halfway deal where you'd spend something to save someone. You blew in.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: You always had a little left. You didn't even blow it all. I spent a lot on guns.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about guys that were really down on their luck? Did you ever see lumberjacks that were really having a rough time making a go of it? They didn't have no money and were just having to borrow money?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No. Because you couldn't go to work any place. No. No. The only thing that put a lumberjack down on their luck would be sickness. Outside of that hell, they could always work. I'll tell you. I've seen the time in Saint Maries work. They'd get mad at you if you didn't go to work. They had a great big... I don't know what he was. I think he was a shoemaker by trade. A very big husky. I think he was a Norwegian. Nationality. A lot of them lumber camps used to put in odors with him for men. He'd try to talk you into going to work. By God, he'd almost get mad when you wouldn't go to work. I'm not ready to go to work yet. He'd talk worse than an insurance statement. Oh, yeah. Don't forget this name now. Brother, that's a key. Yeah. Can you imagine that? Hmm? He was a pest. He was just a pest if you didn't go to work.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: If you weren't ready to go to work, he was a regular pest, will ya? All the logging camps up, the Saint Maries and the St. George River were looking for men, you know. He wasn't really a pest if he ever was one.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did a lot of guys travel around to different camps? I mean, I sort of had the idea that there were two different ways of doing it. Some guys stayed put... You stayed put around Elk River for a long time, didn't you?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah, but that's mostly after I got married. I see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it was... Before you got married, you went around all different places. Yeah.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how come you decided to get married if lumber jacking wasn't a good way to support him?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, wages came up and I got a pretty good job. I got a job as millwright in the planing mill. By that time, I was a pretty good planing mill man. And I got a job as millwright. And I paid for the good wages. But the wages came up to be held during the First World War, too, you know. And that's how I happened to get married.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you meet your wife in Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Mm-mm. She was from Saint Maries. That was my first wife. I got tipped off the bottom of the deck the first time. I got a good life now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So marriages didn't work out in them days either, huh?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No… no, she was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: These days, it seems like half marriages don't work out. When the Depression hit, didn't that make times really tough for the lumberjacks?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. Yes. Yeah… but yeah, secret was tough on the lumberjacks. But let's see now. When is Social Security starting to grow? But it seemed to me like during the latter part of the Depression, there was some workmen's unemployment compensation, wasn't there?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I don't know… the main thing I heard about was the public works stuff, the CCCs and the WPA.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: A lot of guys got out of that. A lot of that. Oh yeah, it was tough, all right. It was tough. I hate to put it tough. But it seemed like there was some kind of work, I don't remember if it was towards the end of the Depression, or there was some kind of workmen's unemployment compensation. The lumberjacks used to call it, he's drawing rocking chair money. Have you ever heard that expression? Yeah. But I don't remember when that started. I want to say he's sitting in a hotel and saying, Mary's drawing rocking chair money.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did you stay at Elk River after the mill shut down?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I don't know. I stayed in Elk River for I think two years. I stayed in Elk River. Then I got, well I had odd jobs. I was forming on the road for a gang. Then I drove a road truck. Then, so on and on, I got a little work now and then, you know, when I raised a big garden and I killed a lot of venison, a lot of it. Then when the blister rust started, they were looking for men. And Jesus, the pay was great those days. I think we got five dollars a day in board or something like that. They were good money those days. I worked in a sixty man camp and I didn't know that they were going to have a hell of a big set up the following year and they were looking for foremen. And everybody in that camp was graded just like a bunch of school kids. Because I didn't know that, you know. Well, that sixty man camp, the ones that got the highest grade was a fellow by the name of James Skeen and I. And I didn't know that until the next year.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the work that they were having you do while you were in that camp?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Eradicate these ribers.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you were pulling the bushes.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. And James Skeen and I, we were tops. So I got a CC foreman job the following summer. Well then after that I just stayed right with them because I got on the field of service.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What were those CC camps like? What were those boys like that they sent out from the east?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, I tell you, they weren't, I had some awful good boys. In my gang I had some awful good boys. For a fact, I don't know that I had any real bad ones. Most of my boys were good boys, but most of my boys were country boys. These were the town bastards that were hard to handle. I had good boys.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your boys come from around Idaho and from around the northwest?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, no… no, I think my boys, a lot of them were from Kentucky. That's the best job I've ever had. You know, I got $140 a month, and the United States government sent me a bill for $15 for board every month. And so the $125 was clear. And you know, those depression prices, they were really something. You know, eggs for a while and dairy were $0.06 a dozen… yeah… i think that's the best job I ever had. If you compare what I earned with what it cost to live. ... You know, he's a Mormon priest.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Really?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah. Simple.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I can't remember who told me that I heard this story about how he went and bopped a robber over the head with a hammer.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, and the robber had a gun.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, he did?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah. Yeah. And he ran across the street and hit him over the head with a hammer. That's how he got to be city marshal.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He wasn't the marshal at that time, huh?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No. No. He was doing some carping to work across the street. And he heard the freak. He ran across the street and heard him over the head with a hammer.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You think Ike was in cahoots with the bootlegging?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, no. Oh, no. No. No. Fair. No. No. No. He wasn't. Oh, no… no. No… no. They didn't. They called it. Or Pearson. Pearson was sitting in marshal and they called it. They were pretty sure they weren't in cahoots with the bootleggers. No, sir. No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you hear that story about the plane that crashed when they were burning the mill?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah… oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What is the way you heard what happened there?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: I just I haven't really heard the story. I just heard something about it that the plane crashed when they were burning the mill down. Yeah. I'll tell you. Let's see. I think I got one of the rings off of that. Off of that. One of the propellers. I don't know if I got it. Yeah. This is one of the rings off of the propeller. Oh, gee. Gee. I got the other rings someplace, too. It's flat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What happened, then? How come the plane crashed right then?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, they got off course. They got off course, you know. And of course, they got radios, you know. And they contacted Spokane. And they said that they were off course. But they were circling a place where there is a big fire. They were burning the mill down. And Spokane contacted all the places that they could in the Inland Empire. And Vilda Polson was telephone operator in in Elk River at the time. And she got it. So she sent the messages back to Spokane, said, they're burning the mill up here at Elk River and there's a plane circling overhead. And then they do where they were. Then they telegraphed to the plane. And they hit for the beam that goes between Kellogg and Missoula, I guess. You know, there's a beam. But they weren't high enough to hit the cemetery ridge.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, no. No, it's a ridge between the big creek drainage and the... What is the name of that river that goes through Kellogg… coeur d 'Alene… the big... It's a big ridge between the big creek drainage and the Coeur d 'Alene river drainage. It's the cemetery ridge. And they hit that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How far from Elk River did they? Were they pretty close to Elk River still when they went down?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, no… no. No, that's... That's quite a ways. They were almost to Kellogg, Idaho.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How'd you get the ring?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: You know, they had a Blisters camp up in Big Creek one year. And it was all Eastern boys. They spent every weekend taking that plane apart and taking parts of it for souvenirs. And they say that when that camp broke up, those boys were just loaded down with things off of that plane. And one of the guys over at the headquarters gave me this ring. He said it comes off of the roller bearings on the propeller. It was what they call it... was it Lockheed Electra? I think that's what it was. A friend of mine, Neil Fullerton, he was the head of timber sale for the St. Joe Forest. He was the head of the party that went in there and got the hand out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, it didn't die, the pilot?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah. They were right in the seats, crows solid, off in the snow. I guess they flew through the window when it hit. And I guess when it hit, they just sheared off great big Tamarack just like they'd been almost cut off with a knife. They were just a little too low. But that's a long way from Elk River by Kellogg. But it was in the Polson that was ... to where they were.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: George, when you got on civil service, where did you go and what did you do when you got on after the blister rust?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, I stayed with the blister rust. I finally quit them. I came to Lewiston and went to work for the Ray girl.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, and then you lived in Lewiston from then on?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And you and your first wife split up by that time, or were you still married?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: No, no. My first wife and I, we split up while I was on civil service. She was from my second wife. She was from North Dakota. She was born in Tacoma. She was one year old when the family moved to North Dakota on the farm. She was raised in North Dakota. I think they had some trouble in that river too. With some black kids. That's one thing when I was at camp for the blister rust. I got all the niggers. Of course, they knew they'd get a fair shake. I have no prejudice against any nationality or any creed or color or anything. The supervisor that we had, he knew that the niggas would get a fair shake at my camp. But I never had any trouble with the niggas. I had a Chevy at that time, and he had an awful good radio in it. Boy, he had a good radio. And when was this? You must have been pretty young. You don't remember when Joe Lewis was fighting somebody.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: You remember Joe Lewis? ... I forget he was fighting. There were a few radios in camp, but they couldn't get a thing. So I finally went out and thought, well, I'll see. Maybe I can get it on my car radio. And it came in like a house of fire. And I just got out of there and nothing flat my car was full of niggas. I had just enough niggas in camp to fill it up. And I just let them have it. Boy, they wanted to see Joe Lewis win. But who he fought, I forgot. He fought them all. They could have been a lot of guys. I forget now. Boy, I tell you when those niggas farmed out that I could get it on my car radio, they just came running.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were your boys, those blacks, were they able to go into town?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They could go into Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh yeah. They were grown men.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Young men?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, they were in the 30s. I'll tell you, I had a couple, three of them there that I wouldn't advise anybody next to be able to tackle them. I had one guy there. He was the toughest huskiest ever making man. Oh, I'll tell you, he was husky. But there's a rule that didn't stay long. Harder than I wanted him to. Oh, I bought him a pair of gloves. You know, on rainy days we'd cut wood and send him to headquarters so that headquarters would have plenty of wood for the winter. And you know, this guy, he split wood. He almost wore the skin out of his hands. I went into town and bought him a damn good pair of buckskin gloves and gave it. Oh, he was at work and son of a bitch, I'll tell you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did these guys go when they had time off? Did they go to Orofino  or Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Elk River. Yeah… they'd probably come from the cities back east. Or maybe from the south, I wonder. I don't know. No, I think they were, I think they came from smaller towns down south. I had two Mexican camps. Very happy, go lucky outfit. The Mexicans. I like him, personally. But it's hard to get any work out of him. If it was a rainy day and we saw wood, you could get a lot of work out of him. And if one of them threw one another glove, then they'd try to out-sow each other or something like that. But outside of that, they, two words, they weren't hard workers. Mexican, they're easy to get along with. I had one Mexican camp, and the other Mexican told me that he was a bandito. And they said, when he could be clothed off at night, his eyes looked like a seam. He'd be shot at with sharpness, but I never had any trouble with him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, it's one thing I was going to ask you about Albert Wiley.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was, was he a dumb kid?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Well, I'll tell you, if you can say that a guy can take a little flour, sugar and salt and a 30-30 carbine, and go out in the woods and live for months, would you call him dumb? I wouldn't either. He just never got used to city ways. Have you ever read The Grapes of Wrath? ... Well, do you remember reading about that guy that stayed the day after everybody pulled out, and he went from house to house, and, and, and just kind of like a recluse after everybody pulled for camp. Well, Albert Wiley was kind of like him. The, the, the happiest days he ever had was when he was a kid on the home bed. And then his father and mother died, and his sister scattered and got married, and Albert was left all alone, and he was just... Well, he was just a pitiful character, you know. I told you about Albert and the moon. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Yeah… i don't know if he's still alive or not. He's, he's got a costume in, in...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's Bob Smith, right?

segments.speaker: George Schmaltz
segments.words: Bob Smith. Yeah, you mentioned him to me. I was going to talk...
